questions.q: How does this lesson precisely define training/serving skew?
options: Any time a model's accuracy drops below 90%
A difference between the feature values a model was trained on and the feature values it sees at serving time for the same logical input
A disagreement between two data scientists about model architecture
The time delay between training a model and deploying it
questions.explain: Skew is specifically about feature value mismatches between training and serving for what should be the same input — not accuracy thresholds or deployment timing.

questions.q: What is "time travel" / data leakage in the context of feature stores?
options: Running a training job on outdated hardware
Joining a feature's current value onto a historical training example, leaking information from after the event into training
Deploying a model before it finishes training
A bug in Feast's materialization scheduler
questions.explain: Time travel happens when a naive join uses a feature's present-day value for a historical row, leaking future information into training that couldn't have been known at the time.

questions.q: What specific guarantee does a point-in-time join provide?
options: It guarantees the model will achieve 100% accuracy
Each historical event is matched to the feature value as of that event's own timestamp, never a later value
It automatically retrains the model every hour
It removes the need for an online store entirely
questions.explain: A point-in-time join's defining guarantee is temporal correctness: matching each row to the feature value that was true at that row's own timestamp, not a more recent one.

questions.q: In the Feast code example, what role does the `event_timestamp` column in `entity_df` play when calling `get_historical_features`?
options: It is ignored; only driver_id matters
It tells Feast which point in time to use when looking up each row's feature value, preventing future data from leaking in
It sets the TTL for the online store
It configures the Redis connection string
questions.explain: event_timestamp is what makes the join point-in-time correct — Feast uses it to retrieve the feature value that was valid at that exact moment, not a later one.

questions.q: How can a team detect skew in a system that is already live, before it shows up as a performance drop?
options: Wait for customer complaints about the product
Log the feature values actually used at serving time and periodically compare them against what the offline pipeline would compute for the same entity and timestamp
Skew cannot be detected until the model is retrained
Delete the online store and rebuild it from scratch
questions.explain: Because skew is a difference between two numbers that should match, it can be directly measured by comparing logged serving-time values against the offline pipeline's computed value for the same entity and timestamp.
